intro.html: Ten verbs for getting in the way, from a little to a lot. Some only slow things down (hinder, hamper, impede, encumber). Some block them (obstruct, stymie) or defeat a plan (thwart). One holds back from inside (inhibit). Two stop things before they start (preclude, forestall).
Strength matters. Mud that impedes you slows you down; a locked door that precludes entry makes it impossible. Forestall means acting early, stepping in front of a problem before it arrives.

words.def: to get in the way of; to slow down
words.ex: The puppy tugging at her backpack {hindered} Ivy’s walk to the bus.
words.ctx: Heavy snow {hindered} the rescue, but it did not stop it; the team simply moved more slowly and reached the cabin by dark.
words.etym: From Old English hindrian, “to hold back,” related to hind and behind.

mn.text: Ivy tries to walk to the bus, but the puppy hangs onto her backpack from behind. The puppy {hinders} her.

scene.alt: A puppy tugs at a girl’s backpack from behind as she tries to walk to the bus.

words.def: to hold back or slow down progress
words.ex: The giant picnic basket {hampered} Dev’s climb up the hill.
words.ctx: A shortage of buses {hampered} the school’s field trips all year; classes had to take turns, and some never left the building at all.
words.note: A different word, the noun hamper, is a large basket for picnics or laundry.

mn.cue: a heavy HAMPER slows the hike
mn.text: Dev lugs the huge picnic hamper up the steep hill, one slow step at a time. The heavy basket {hampers} his climb.

scene.alt: A teen struggles uphill carrying an enormous picnic basket.

words.def: to slow or block movement or progress
words.ex: Thick mud {impeded} the hikers at every step.
words.ctx: Fallen branches {impeded} the river’s flow, so the water rose behind them and spread across the meadow.
words.etym: From Latin impedire, “to shackle the feet”: in + pes, ped- (foot).

mn.cue: IM-PED: FEET caught in the mud
mn.text: Pip’s boots sink deep into the mud, and every step is a struggle. The mud {impedes} him: it catches his feet.

scene.alt: A boy in a raincoat struggles to pull his feet out of deep mud.

words.def: to block a path, passage or view
words.ex: A fallen tree {obstructed} the road to the lake.
words.ctx: The new billboard {obstructs} the view from the old inn; guests who once watched the sunset over the bay now stare at a giant sign.
words.etym: From Latin obstruere, “to build against, block”: ob (against) + struere (to pile up, build).

mn.cue: OB-STRUCT: a STRUCTURE in the way
mn.text: A huge log lies across the road like a wall, and the bus cannot get past. The log {obstructs} the road.

scene.alt: A bus driver scratches his head at a huge log blocking the road.

words.def: to stop someone from carrying out a plan
words.ex: The goalie {thwarted} every shot in the second half.
words.ctx: The squirrels’ plan to raid the bird feeder was {thwarted} by a slippery metal pole that none of them could climb.
words.etym: From Old Norse thvert, “across”: to thwart is to cut across someone’s path.

mn.cue: THWACK! the goalie THWARTS the shot
mn.text: Dev winds up for the winning goal, but Maya leaps and thwacks the ball away. She {thwarts} his plan.

scene.alt: A goalie leaps and knocks away a shot as the shooter looks shocked.

words.ex: Shyness {inhibited} Lila from raising her hand, though she knew the answer.
words.ctx: Cold weather {inhibits} the growth of the vines; the grapes stay small and sour until the warm days of late summer.
words.etym: From Latin inhibere, “to hold back”: in + habere (to hold).

mn.text: Lila knows the answer, but shyness holds her in, and her hand stays down. Shyness {inhibits} her.

scene.alt: A shy girl keeps her hand down, though she knows the answer, while classmates raise theirs.

words.def: to weigh down with a burden
words.ex: The hikers were {encumbered} by tents, pots and three days of food.
words.ctx: The young couple’s plans were {encumbered} by debt; every dollar they earned went to old bills instead of the house they dreamed of.
words.etym: From Old French encombrer, “to block up, burden.”

mn.text: Sven staggers home with a giant crate of a hundred cucumbers in his arms. He is {encumbered}: so weighed down he can barely move.

scene.alt: A big man staggers under the weight of a huge crate of cucumbers.

words.def: to block completely; to leave stuck or stumped
words.ex: The last riddle in the book {stymied} the whole family.
words.ctx: Engineers were {stymied} for months: every design for the bridge failed the wind test, and no one could figure out why.
words.etym: First a golf word of the 1800s: a stymie was a ball lying in the line between another ball and the hole.

mn.cue: STY-MIE: the pig blocks the STY
mn.text: The giant pig flops across the gate of its sty, and no matter what Farmer Omar tries, he cannot get in. He is {stymied}.

scene.alt: A big pig sleeps across the gate of its pen while a puzzled farmer scratches his head.

words.def: to make impossible in advance; to rule out
words.ex: The locked gate {precluded} any visit to the garden.
words.ctx: Her broken wrist {precluded} playing in the final, so she spent the game on the bench, cheering louder than anyone.
words.etym: From Latin praecludere, “to shut off”: prae (before) + claudere (to shut).
words.note: Preclude is stronger than hinder: it rules something out completely, ahead of time.

mn.text: The museum door was locked before anyone arrived, so no one could get in at all. The locked door {precluded} any visit.

scene.alt: A boy and his grandmother sadly face a locked door with a closed sign.

words.def: to prevent something by acting first
words.ex: Mom {forestalled} a meltdown by handing out snacks before the kids got hungry.
words.ctx: To {forestall} complaints about the noise, the band visited every neighbor a week before the party and invited them all to come.

mn.cue: FORE-STALL: stop it BEFORE it starts
mn.text: Just before the kids get hungry and cranky, Mom hands out sandwiches. She {forestalls} the meltdown.

scene.alt: A mother hands out sandwiches to two happy children just before snack time.

head: how much it gets in the way
words
rows: rules it out ahead of time
heads it off by acting first
after.cap: From slowing down to ruling out.

after.html: Two words have a Latin foot in them: impede (in + ped, foot: to tangle the feet) and its opposite expedite (ex + ped: to free the feet). One has a Latin door: preclude (pre + clud, shut).

items.q: Which is stronger: to hinder a trip or to preclude it?
choices: to preclude it: it becomes impossible
to hinder it: it becomes impossible
items.why: To hinder is to slow down; to preclude is to make impossible ahead of time.

items.q: The coach called a time-out before the other team could build a lead. She was trying to ______ a comeback.
items.why: To forestall is to prevent something by acting first.

items.q: Which word comes from Latin words meaning “to shackle the feet”?
items.why: Impede: in + ped (foot). Its opposite, expedite, means to free the feet.

items.q: True or false: a truck parked across a driveway obstructs it.
items.why: True. To obstruct is to block a path or passage.
